statement: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and $A$ a [star-algebra](c:star-algebra) of [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) on $H$ that contains the identity. Then $A''$, the [commutant](c:commutant) of its commutant, is the closure of $A$ in the [weak operator topology](c:weak-operator-topology) and in the [strong operator topology](c:strong-operator-topology). So $A$ is a [von Neumann algebra](c:von-neumann-algebra) exactly when $A = A''$.

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The set $A \subseteq B(H)$ is a subalgebra that is closed under adjoints.
The algebra $A$ contains the identity operator $I$.

conclusion: $A''$ equals the weak and the strong operator closure of $A$; in particular $A$ is weakly closed if and only if $A = A''$.

proofs.name: Cyclic projection and amplification
proofs.slogan: Approximate an operator of the bicommutant at finitely many vectors through the projection onto a cyclic subspace and an amplification to $H^n$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every Hilbert space. The identity is needed: $A''$ always contains $I$, while the closure of a non-unital $A$ may not.

roles.why: Every closed subspace of a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) has an [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection).
Closure under adjoints makes the projection onto an invariant subspace commute with $A$.
The identity in $A$ puts the vector $\xi$ inside $\overline{A\xi}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every commutant is closed in the [weak operator topology](c:weak-operator-topology).
steps.detail: For $S \subseteq B(H)$, $S' = \bigcap_{s \in S} \{x : xs = sx\}$, and each map $x \mapsto \langle (xs - sx)\xi, \eta \rangle$ is weakly continuous. So $A''$ is weakly closed, and it contains $A$, so it contains the weak closure of $A$.

steps.slogan: Compare the strong closure of $A$ with its weak closure.
steps.detail: The bound $|\langle (x - a)\xi, \eta \rangle| \le \|(x - a)\xi\|\,\|\eta\|$ shows that the [strong operator topology](c:strong-operator-topology) is finer than the weak one. So the strong closure of $A$ lies in its weak closure.

steps.slogan: Approximate $x \in A''$ at one vector $\xi$ through the projection onto $\overline{A\xi}$.
steps.detail: The closed subspace $K = \overline{A\xi}$ is invariant under $A$ and under all adjoints, so its [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) $P$ lies in $A'$. Then $xP = Px$, and $\xi = I\xi \in K$ gives $x\xi = xP\xi = Px\xi \in K$, a limit of vectors $a\xi$ with $a \in A$.

steps.slogan: Amplify to $H^n$ to approximate $x$ at finitely many vectors at once.
steps.detail: Let $A$ act diagonally on $H^n$; this is again a unital star-algebra. Its commutant consists of the $n \times n$ matrices with entries in $A'$, which commute with $x \oplus \dots \oplus x$. Step 3 at $(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n)$ gives $a \in A$ with $\sum_i \|(x - a)\xi_i\|^2 < \varepsilon^2$, so $x$ lies in the strong closure of $A$.

steps.slogan: Chain the three inclusions into the equality of $A''$ and both closures.
steps.detail: Steps 1, 2 and 4 give $A'' \subseteq \overline{A}^{s} \subseteq \overline{A}^{w} \subseteq A''$, so the three sets are equal. Hence $A$ is weakly closed exactly when $A = A''$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The Hilbert space supplies orthogonal projections onto closed subspaces.
concepts.c:star-algebra: Closure under adjoints makes invariant subspaces reduce the algebra.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: The algebra and its commutants live inside the bounded operators.
concepts.c:commutant: The projection onto a cyclic subspace lies in the commutant.
concepts.c:weak-operator-topology: Commutants are weakly closed, which gives one inclusion.
concepts.c:strong-operator-topology: The approximation at finitely many vectors is strong convergence.
concepts.c:von-neumann-algebra: A von Neumann algebra is a weakly closed unital star-algebra of operators.
concepts.c:orthogonal-projection: The projection onto the closure of $A\xi$ carries the approximation.

source.note: Von Neumann's double commutant theorem with its standard proof, as in G. J. Murphy, C*-Algebras and Operator Theory, section 4.1.

statement: A function $\varphi\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is continuous and [positive-definite](c:positive-definite-function) if and only if $\varphi(x) = \int e^{i x \cdot \xi}\, d\mu(\xi)$ for a positive [finite measure](c:finite-measure) $\mu$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, that is, $\varphi$ is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of $\mu$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\varphi$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The function $\varphi$ is [positive-definite](c:positive-definite-function): $\sum_{j,k} c_j \overline{c_k}\, \varphi(x_j - x_k) \ge 0$ for all finitely many points $x_j$ and complex numbers $c_j$.

conclusion: There is a positive finite Borel measure $\mu$ with $\varphi(x) = \int e^{i x \cdot \xi}\, d\mu(\xi)$; conversely every such transform is continuous and positive-definite.

proofs.name: Gaussian regularization
proofs.slogan: Damp $\varphi$ by a Gaussian, show that the damped function has a nonnegative integrable Fourier density, and remove the damping by Lévy's continuity theorem.
proofs.scope: Both directions on $\mathbb{R}^n$; the case $\varphi(0) = 0$ gives $\varphi = 0$ and $\mu = 0$. The version on a [locally compact abelian group](c:locally-compact-abelian-group) needs Haar measure and Gelfand theory and is not covered.

roles.why: Continuity turns finite positive sums into double integrals and gives the continuity at 0 that Lévy's theorem needs.
Positive-definiteness bounds $\varphi$ by $\varphi(0)$ and makes the regularized Fourier density nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Check that the transform of a positive finite measure is continuous and positive-definite.
steps.detail: If $\varphi = \hat\mu$, then $\sum_{j,k} c_j \overline{c_k}\, \varphi(x_j - x_k) = \int |\sum_j c_j e^{i x_j \cdot \xi}|^2 \, d\mu(\xi) \ge 0$. Continuity follows from dominated convergence with the constant bound $\mu(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|\varphi|$ by $\varphi(0)$ with the positive-definite $2 \times 2$ matrices.
steps.detail: One point gives $\varphi(0) \ge 0$. The points $0$ and $x$ give a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with entries $\varphi(0), \varphi(x), \varphi(-x), \varphi(0)$, so $\varphi(-x) = \overline{\varphi(x)}$ and $|\varphi(x)| \le \varphi(0)$. If $\varphi(0) = 0$, then $\varphi = 0$ and $\mu = 0$ works.

steps.slogan: Pass from finite sums to $\iint \varphi(x - y) f(x) \overline{f(y)}\, dx\, dy \ge 0$.
steps.detail: For continuous compactly supported $f$, the Riemann sums $\sum_{j,k} \varphi(x_j - x_k) f(x_j) \overline{f(x_k)}\, \Delta^2$ over cells of volume $\Delta$ are nonnegative and converge to the double integral, because $\varphi$ is continuous and bounded. A limit extends the inequality to $f$ with Gaussian decay.

steps.slogan: Insert $f(x) = e^{-\varepsilon |x|^2 - i x \cdot \xi}$ to get a nonnegative density $p_\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Substitute $u = x - y$ and $v = x + y$, so that $|x|^2 + |y|^2 = (|u|^2 + |v|^2)/2$, and integrate out $v$ by Fubini. This gives $p_\varepsilon(\xi) = (2\pi)^{-n} \int \varphi(u) e^{-\varepsilon |u|^2/2} e^{-i u \cdot \xi}\, du \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p_\varepsilon$ has total mass $\varphi(0)$ and inverts to $\varphi(x) e^{-\varepsilon |x|^2/2}$.
steps.detail: The integral of $p_\varepsilon(\xi) e^{-\delta |\xi|^2/2}$ is the average of $\varphi(u) e^{-\varepsilon |u|^2/2}$ against a Gaussian kernel of width $\sqrt{\delta}$, which tends to $\varphi(0)$; monotone convergence gives $\int p_\varepsilon = \varphi(0)$. Fourier inversion then gives $\varphi(x) e^{-\varepsilon |x|^2/2} = \int e^{i x \cdot \xi} p_\varepsilon(\xi)\, d\xi$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon \to 0$ and take the weak limit by Lévy's continuity theorem.
steps.detail:
The probability measures $p_\varepsilon\, d\xi / \varphi(0)$ have [characteristic functions](c:characteristic-function) $\varphi(x) e^{-\varepsilon |x|^2/2} / \varphi(0)$, which converge pointwise to $\varphi / \varphi(0)$, a function continuous at 0. Lévy's theorem gives a weak limit $
u$ with $\hat
u = \varphi / \varphi(0)$, so $\mu = \varphi(0)
u$ works.

steps.slogan: Combine the converse with the construction into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the direction from measures to functions. Steps 2 to 6 give, for each continuous positive-definite $\varphi$, a positive finite measure $\mu$ with $\hat\mu = \varphi$.

concepts.c:positive-definite-function: Positive-definiteness is what makes the regularized density nonnegative.
concepts.c:finite-measure: The representing measure has total mass $\varphi(0)$.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The theorem identifies $\varphi$ as the Fourier transform of a measure.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Lévy's theorem acts on the characteristic functions of the approximating measures.
concepts.c:locally-compact-abelian-group: The general version replaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ by such a group.

source.note: The standard proof by Gaussian regularization, Fourier inversion and Lévy's continuity theorem.

statement: Let $k$ be an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) and $F, G \in k[X, Y, Z]$ [homogeneous polynomials](c:homogeneous-polynomial) of degrees $m, n \ge 1$ with no common factor. Then the [algebraic curves](c:algebraic-curve) $F = 0$ and $G = 0$ in the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) meet in finitely many points, and $\sum_P I(P, F \cap G) = mn$, where $I$ is the [intersection multiplicity](c:intersection-multiplicity).

hypotheses.text: The field $k$ is [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field).
The polynomials $F$ and $G$ are [homogeneous](c:homogeneous-polynomial) of degrees $m \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$.
The polynomials $F$ and $G$ have no common nonconstant factor.

conclusion: The two curves meet in finitely many points, and their intersection multiplicities at these points add up to $mn$.

proofs.name: Dimension count in a graded quotient
proofs.slogan: Express the sum of local intersection numbers as the dimension of one graded piece of $k[X,Y,Z]/(F,G)$, which an exact sequence fixes at $mn$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $I(P, F \cap G) = \dim_k \mathcal{O}_P/(f, g)$ for the affine equations $f, g$ at $P$. A common factor gives infinitely many common points, so coprimality is necessary.

roles.why: Algebraic closure makes $k$ infinite, splits binary forms into linear factors and gives the Nullstellensatz.
The degrees fix the shifts in the exact sequence and the value $mn$ of the count.
Coprimality gives finitely many common points and exactness in the middle of the sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that the two curves have only finitely many common points.
steps.detail: In an affine chart the equations $f, g$ stay coprime in $k(x)[y]$ by Gauss's lemma, so $af + bg = d(x)$ with $0 \ne d \in k[x]$. Hence the common zeros have finitely many $x$-coordinates, and in the same way finitely many $y$-coordinates.

steps.slogan: Move a line that misses all common points to the line $Z = 0$.
steps.detail: The field is infinite and the common points are finitely many, so some line avoids them; a projective change of coordinates makes it $Z = 0$. Intersection numbers do not change, and all common points now lie in the affine plane $Z = 1$.

steps.slogan: Write the sum of intersection numbers as $\dim_k k[x,y]/(f,g)$ with $f = F(x,y,1)$, $g = G(x,y,1)$.
steps.detail: The ideal $(f, g)$ has finitely many zeros, so the Nullstellensatz and the Chinese remainder theorem give $k[x,y]/(f,g) \cong \prod_P \mathcal{O}_P/(f,g)$ with the [local rings](c:local-ring) $\mathcal{O}_P$ at the common points. Taking dimensions gives $\sum_P I(P, F \cap G)$.

steps.slogan: Write the [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0 \to \Gamma_{d-m-n} \to \Gamma_{d-m} \oplus \Gamma_{d-n} \to \Gamma_d \to (\Gamma/(F,G))_d \to 0$.
steps.detail: Here $\Gamma_e$ is the space of forms of degree $e$, and the maps are $C \mapsto (CG, -CF)$ and $(A, B) \mapsto AF + BG$. Exactness in the middle holds because $AF = -BG$ in the [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain) $k[X,Y,Z]$ with $F, G$ coprime forces $A = CG$ and $B = -CF$.

steps.slogan: Count dimensions to get $\dim (\Gamma/(F,G))_d = mn$ for $d \ge m + n$.
steps.detail: With $\dim \Gamma_e = (e+1)(e+2)/2$, the alternating sum $\dim\Gamma_d - \dim\Gamma_{d-m} - \dim\Gamma_{d-n} + \dim\Gamma_{d-m-n}$ is a second difference, with steps $m$ and $n$, of a quadratic with leading coefficient $1/2$. So it equals $mn$.

steps.slogan: Show that dehomogenization maps $(\Gamma/(F,G))_d$ isomorphically onto $k[x,y]/(f,g)$ for $d \ge m + n$.
steps.detail: No common point lies on $Z = 0$, so the binary forms $F(X,Y,0)$ and $G(X,Y,0)$ are nonzero and share no linear factor, and $Z$ is a nonzerodivisor on $\Gamma/(F,G)$. Multiplication by $Z$ is then injective between pieces of equal dimension $mn$, hence bijective, which makes dehomogenization injective and surjective.

steps.slogan: Combine the local sum with the graded count to get $mn$.
steps.detail: Steps 3, 5 and 6 give $\sum_P I(P, F \cap G) = \dim_k k[x,y]/(f,g) = \dim_k (\Gamma/(F,G))_d = mn$. Step 1 gives the finiteness of the set of common points.

concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure makes every common zero visible and the field infinite.
concepts.c:homogeneous-polynomial: Homogeneity gives the graded pieces that the count measures.
concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The theorem counts the common points of two plane curves.
concepts.c:projective-plane: In the projective plane no intersection escapes to infinity.
concepts.c:intersection-multiplicity: Each common point counts with its local multiplicity.
concepts.c:local-ring: The local ring at a point measures its intersection multiplicity.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The exact sequence turns the dimension into an alternating sum.
concepts.c:unique-factorization-domain: Unique factorization gives exactness in the middle of the sequence.

source.note: The graded dimension count of W. Fulton, Algebraic Curves, section 5.3.

statement: Let $\mu^*$ be an [outer measure](c:outer-measure) on a set $X$. The sets $A$ with $\mu^*(E) = \mu^*(E \cap A) + \mu^*(E \setminus A)$ for every $E \subseteq X$ form a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{M}$, and $\mu^*$ is a complete [measure](c:measure) on $\mathcal{M}$. If $\mu^*$ comes from a [pre-measure](c:pre-measure) $\mu_0$ on a [ring of sets](c:is-set-ring), then $\mathcal{M}$ contains the ring and the measure extends $\mu_0$.

hypotheses.text: The map $\mu^*$ is an [outer measure](c:outer-measure): $\mu^*(\emptyset) = 0$, and $\mu^*$ is monotone and countably subadditive.
For the extension part, $\mu^*(E) = \inf \sum_i \mu_0(B_i)$ over all countable covers of $E$ by sets $B_i$ of a ring $\mathcal{R}$ on which $\mu_0$ is a [pre-measure](c:pre-measure).

conclusion: $\mathcal{M}$ is a σ-algebra and $\mu^*|_{\mathcal{M}}$ is a complete measure; in the induced case $\mathcal{R} \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ and $\mu^* = \mu_0$ on $\mathcal{R}$.

proofs.name: Carathéodory's splitting criterion
proofs.slogan: Check the splitting identity under complements, finite unions and countable disjoint unions, then test the ring sets with near-optimal covers.
proofs.scope: Both parts; the second part assumes that $\mu^*$ is induced by $\mu_0$. A test set with $\mu^*(E) = \infty$ satisfies every splitting inequality, so only $\mu^*(E) < \infty$ needs work.

roles.why: Subadditivity gives one inequality of each splitting identity, and monotonicity handles null sets and limits.
Near-optimal covers by ring sets compare $\mu^*$ with $\mu_0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the splitting sets form an [algebra of sets](c:algebra-of-sets).
steps.detail: The identity is symmetric in $A$ and $X \setminus A$, and $\emptyset$ satisfies it. For $A, B \in \mathcal{M}$, split $E$ by $A$ and then $E \setminus A$ by $B$; subadditivity gives $\mu^*(E) \ge \mu^*(E \cap (A \cup B)) + \mu^*(E \setminus (A \cup B))$, and the reverse inequality is subadditivity again.

steps.slogan: Split a test set by a countable disjoint union of splitting sets.
steps.detail: Let $A = \bigsqcup_i A_i$ with $A_i \in \mathcal{M}$ and $B_n = A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$. Induction and monotonicity give $\mu^*(E) \ge \sum_{i \le n} \mu^*(E \cap A_i) + \mu^*(E \setminus A)$; letting $n \to \infty$ and using subadditivity gives $A \in \mathcal{M}$, and $E = A$ gives countable additivity.

steps.slogan: Show that every set of outer measure zero is a splitting set.
steps.detail: If $\mu^*(N) = 0$, monotonicity gives $\mu^*(E \cap N) + \mu^*(E \setminus N) \le 0 + \mu^*(E)$, and subadditivity gives the reverse. Every subset of $N$ also has outer measure zero, so the measure is complete.

steps.slogan: Test a ring set $A$ against a test set $E$ with a near-optimal cover of $E$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $B_i \in \mathcal{R}$ covering $E$ with $\sum_i \mu_0(B_i) \le \mu^*(E) + \varepsilon$. The ring sets $B_i \cap A$ and $B_i \setminus A$ cover $E \cap A$ and $E \setminus A$, and additivity of $\mu_0$ gives $\mu^*(E \cap A) + \mu^*(E \setminus A) \le \mu^*(E) + \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mu^*$ equals the [pre-measure](c:pre-measure) $\mu_0$ on the ring.
steps.detail: The cover $\{A\}$ gives $\mu^*(A) \le \mu_0(A)$. For a cover $A \subseteq \bigcup_i B_i$ by ring sets, the disjoint ring sets $C_i = (A \cap B_i) \setminus \bigcup_{j<i} B_j$ have union $A$, so countable additivity and monotonicity of $\mu_0$ give $\mu_0(A) = \sum_i \mu_0(C_i) \le \sum_i \mu_0(B_i)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the closure properties into a complete measure that extends $\mu_0$.
steps.detail: A countable union of sets $A_i$ of the algebra is the disjoint union of the sets $A_i \setminus (A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_{i-1})$, so step 2 makes $\mathcal{M}$ a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) with $\mu^*$ countably additive on it. Steps 3 to 5 add completeness, $\mathcal{R} \subseteq \mathcal{M}$ and $\mu^* = \mu_0$ on $\mathcal{R}$.

concepts.c:outer-measure: The outer measure is the raw set function that the construction restricts.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The splitting sets form the σ-algebra of the new measure.
concepts.c:measure: Restricted to the splitting sets, the outer measure is countably additive.
concepts.c:pre-measure: The pre-measure on the ring induces the outer measure and is extended.
concepts.c:is-set-ring: Covers by ring sets define the induced outer measure.
concepts.c:algebra-of-sets: Closure under complements and finite unions comes before countable unions.

source.note: The standard proof, as in G. B. Folland, Real Analysis, theorem 1.11 and proposition 1.13 (stated there for an algebra of sets).

statement: Let $f$ be continuous on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$ and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z - c| < R$. Then every $w$ with $|w - c| < R$ satisfies $f(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \oint_{|z - c| = R} \frac{f(z)}{z - w}\, dz$, a [contour integral](c:contour-integral) over the positively oriented circle.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous on the closed disc $|z - c| \le R$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z - c| < R$.
The point $w$ lies in the open disc: $|w - c| < R$.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general: $f$ takes values in a complex Banach space and may fail to be differentiable at countably many points of the open disc.

proofs.name: Difference quotient and Cauchy's theorem
proofs.slogan: Cauchy's theorem makes the integral of the difference quotient $(f(z) - f(w))/(z - w)$ vanish, and the kernel $1/(z - w)$ integrates to $2\pi i$.
proofs.scope: The formula for a circle; a general Jordan curve needs a general Cauchy theorem. mathlib also extends the formula by continuity to countably many bad points, which is not needed here.

roles.why: Continuity on the closed disc makes the difference quotient continuous up to the circle, as Cauchy's theorem needs.
Holomorphy makes the [difference quotient](c:difference-quotient) holomorphic off $w$ and continuous at $w$.
A point inside the circle gives $\oint dz/(z - w) = 2\pi i$ and keeps $z - w \ne 0$ on the circle.

steps.slogan: Form the [difference quotient](c:difference-quotient) $F(z) = (f(z) - f(w))/(z - w)$ with $F(w) = f'(w)$.
steps.detail: Because $f$ is differentiable at $w$, $F$ is continuous at $w$. So $F$ is continuous on the closed disc and [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) at every point of the open disc except possibly $w$.

steps.slogan: Show by Cauchy's integral theorem that $\oint_{|z - c| = R} F(z)\, dz = 0$.
steps.detail: Cauchy's theorem for a disc holds for functions continuous on the closed disc and holomorphic off a countable set, here the single point $w$. So the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) of $F$ vanishes.

steps.slogan: Compute $\oint_{|z - c| = R} dz/(z - w) = 2\pi i$ for $|w - c| < R$.
steps.detail: At $w = c$ the parametrization $z = c + Re^{i\theta}$ gives $\int_0^{2\pi} i\, d\theta = 2\pi i$. As a function of $w$ in the disc the integral has derivative $\oint dz/(z - w)^2 = 0$, because $(z - w)^{-2}$ has a primitive on the circle, so it is constant.

steps.slogan: Split $f(z)/(z - w)$ as $F(z) + f(w)/(z - w)$ and integrate both terms.
steps.detail: On the circle $z \ne w$, so $f(z)/(z - w) = F(z) + f(w)/(z - w)$. Steps 2 and 3 give $\oint f(z)/(z - w)\, dz = 0 + 2\pi i\, f(w)$; division by $2\pi i$ gives the formula.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy at $w$ removes the singularity of the difference quotient.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The formula and Cauchy's theorem are statements about integrals over the circle.
concepts.c:difference-quotient: The difference quotient is the function to which Cauchy's theorem applies.

statement: Let $X_n$ and $X$ be [random variables](c:random-variable) with values in a topological space $E$ with its Borel sets, and let $g\colon E \to F$ be a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map to a topological space $F$. If $X_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $X$, then $g(X_n)$ converges in distribution to $g(X)$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $X_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $X$: $\mathbb{E}\, h(X_n) \to \mathbb{E}\, h(X)$ for every [bounded continuous function](c:bounded-continuous-function) $h$ on $E$.
The map $g\colon E \to F$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

formal.difference: The declaration indexes the family by any filter instead of a sequence and lets each random variable live on its own probability space; otherwise it states the same.

proofs.name: Composed test functions
proofs.slogan: A bounded continuous test function on $F$ composed with $g$ is a bounded continuous test function on $E$.
proofs.scope: Convergence in distribution with $g$ continuous everywhere. The versions for convergence in probability, almost sure convergence, or $g$ with a null set of discontinuities are not covered.

roles.why: Convergence of $X_n$ is tested on the composed function $h \circ g$.
Continuity keeps $h \circ g$ continuous and makes $g$ Borel measurable.

steps.slogan: Check that $g(X_n)$ and $g(X)$ are random variables with values in $F$.
steps.detail: A continuous map pulls open sets back to open sets, so it is Borel measurable. A composition of measurable maps is measurable, so $g \circ X_n$ and $g \circ X$ are [random variables](c:random-variable).

steps.slogan: Compose a [bounded continuous function](c:bounded-continuous-function) $h$ on $F$ with $g$.
steps.detail: The composition $h \circ g$ is continuous as a composition of [continuous](c:continuous-function) maps, and $|h \circ g| \le \sup |h|$. So $h \circ g$ is a bounded continuous function on $E$.

steps.slogan: Pass the test function $h \circ g$ through the convergence of $X_n$.
steps.detail: The law of $g(X_n)$ is the [pushforward measure](c:pushforward-measure) of the law of $X_n$ under $g$, so $\mathbb{E}\, h(g(X_n)) = \mathbb{E}\, (h \circ g)(X_n)$. Convergence in distribution gives $\mathbb{E}\, (h \circ g)(X_n) \to \mathbb{E}\, (h \circ g)(X) = \mathbb{E}\, h(g(X))$.

steps.slogan: Conclude convergence in distribution of $g(X_n)$ because $h$ was arbitrary.
steps.detail: Step 3 holds for every bounded continuous $h$ on $F$, and step 1 makes $g(X_n)$ and $g(X)$ random variables. This is the definition of $g(X_n) \to g(X)$ in distribution.

concepts.c:random-variable: The theorem transforms random variables by a fixed map.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity keeps composed test functions continuous.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: This mode of convergence is defined by bounded continuous test functions.
concepts.c:bounded-continuous-function: Test functions on $F$ pull back to test functions on $E$.
concepts.c:pushforward-measure: The law of $g(X_n)$ is the pushforward of the law of $X_n$.

statement: An $n \times n$ real matrix is [doubly stochastic](c:doubly-stochastic-matrix), with nonnegative entries and all row and column sums equal to 1, if and only if it is a convex combination of $n \times n$ [permutation matrices](c:permutation-matrix). So the doubly stochastic matrices form the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of the permutation matrices.
conclusion: The set of $n \times n$ doubly stochastic matrices equals the convex hull of the $n!$ permutation matrices.

formal.difference: The declaration holds over any linearly ordered field and for matrices indexed by any finite type; over the reals it states the same.

proofs.name: Peeling off permutations by Hall's theorem
proofs.slogan: Find by Hall's theorem a permutation inside the support, subtract it with the smallest selected entry, and induct on the number of nonzero entries.
proofs.scope: Both inclusions, for every $n$; for $n = 0$ both sets hold only the empty matrix. The induction runs over nonnegative matrices whose row and column sums all equal one value $s \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Check that every [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) is doubly stochastic.
steps.detail: The matrix $P_\sigma$ has entry 1 at $(i, \sigma(i))$ and 0 elsewhere. Each row and each column holds exactly one 1, so the entries are nonnegative and all row and column sums are 1.

steps.slogan: Show that the doubly stochastic matrices form a [convex set](c:convex-set) that contains the hull.
steps.detail: The set is cut out by linear equations for the row and column sums and by the inequalities $x_{ij} \ge 0$, so convex combinations stay in it. It contains the permutation matrices, so it contains their [convex hull](c:convex-hull).

steps.slogan: Find a permutation $\sigma$ with $M_{i\sigma(i)} > 0$ for all $i$ by Hall's theorem.
steps.detail: Let $M \ge 0$ have all row and column sums $s > 0$. For a set $A$ of rows with nonzero columns $N(A)$, the entries of the rows in $A$ sum to $|A|s$ and lie in the columns $N(A)$, whose entries sum to $|N(A)|s$; so $|A| \le |N(A)|$. Hall's theorem gives a perfect [matching](c:matching) of rows to columns.

steps.slogan: Subtract $cP_\sigma$, where $c$ is the smallest of the entries $M_{i\sigma(i)}$.
steps.detail: The matrix $N = M - cP_\sigma$ has nonnegative entries and all row and column sums $s - c \ge 0$. It has fewer nonzero entries than $M$, because the minimal entry becomes 0 and no zero entry changes.

steps.slogan: Induct on the number of nonzero entries to write $M = \sum_\sigma w_\sigma P_\sigma$ with $w_\sigma \ge 0$.
steps.detail: If $s = 0$, then $M = 0$ and all weights are 0. Otherwise steps 3 and 4 give a matrix $N$ with fewer nonzero entries, strong induction decomposes $N$, and adding back $cP_\sigma$ decomposes $M$.

steps.slogan: Read off one row sum to see that the weights add up to 1.
steps.detail: For a doubly stochastic $M$ the common sum is $s = 1$, and each $P_\sigma$ has row sums 1, so $1 = \sum_\sigma w_\sigma$. So $M$ lies in the convex hull, and with step 2 the two sets are equal.

concepts.c:doubly-stochastic-matrix: These matrices are the set that the theorem describes.
concepts.c:permutation-matrix: Permutation matrices are the pieces peeled off one at a time.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The theorem identifies the doubly stochastic set as a convex hull.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of the doubly stochastic set gives the easy inclusion.
concepts.c:matching: A perfect matching in the support graph is the permutation to subtract.

statement: Let $H$ be a [graph](c:graph) with [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) $\chi(H) = r + 1 \ge 2$. Then the [extremal number](c:extremal-number) $\mathrm{ex}(n, H)$, the largest number of edges of an $n$-vertex graph with no copy of $H$, satisfies $\mathrm{ex}(n, H) = (1 - 1/r + o(1))\, n^2/2$ as $n \to \infty$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $H$ has [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) $r + 1$ with $r \ge 1$, so $H$ has at least one edge.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the minimum-degree form: for $\varepsilon > 0$, every large $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree at least $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon)n$ contains $K_{r+1}(t)$. The edge-count reduction and the Turán lower bound are not in it.

proofs.name: Minimum-degree induction and pigeonhole
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a subgraph of large minimum degree, find a complete $r$-partite subgraph by induction, and extend it by pigeonhole to $K_{r+1}(t)$.
proofs.scope: Both bounds; the upper bound is first proved for $K_{r+1}(t)$, which contains $H$. All estimates are for fixed $r$, $t$ and $\varepsilon$ with $n$ large.

roles.why: An $(r + 1)$-colouring puts $H$ inside $K_{r+1}(t)$, and $\chi(H) > r$ keeps $H$ out of every $r$-partite graph.

steps.slogan: Embed $H$ in the complete $(r+1)$-partite graph $K_{r+1}(t)$ with $t = |V(H)|$.
steps.detail: The $r + 1$ colour classes of $H$ have at most $t$ vertices each, and every edge of $H$ joins two classes. Placing each class in its own part embeds $H$ in $K_{r+1}(t)$, so a graph that contains $K_{r+1}(t)$ contains $H$.

steps.slogan: Count the edges of the [Turán graph](c:turan-graph) $T_r(n)$, which has no copy of $H$.
steps.detail: The graph $T_r(n)$ is complete $r$-partite with parts of sizes $\lfloor n/r \rfloor$ or $\lceil n/r \rceil$, so each subgraph has chromatic number at most $r$ and $H \not\subseteq T_r(n)$. It has at least $(1 - 1/r)\, n^2/2 - r/8$ edges, so $\mathrm{ex}(n, H) \ge (1 - 1/r - o(1))\, n^2/2$.

steps.slogan: Delete vertices of low degree to pass from many edges to a large minimum degree.
steps.detail: Let $e(G) \ge (1 - 1/r + \varepsilon)\, n^2/2$ and delete, one at a time, a vertex of degree below $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon/2)$ times the current order. Summing the losses shows that $m$ remaining vertices span more than $\varepsilon n^2/4 - n$ edges, so $m^2 > \varepsilon n^2/2 - 2n$; the process stops at a subgraph of minimum degree $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon/2)m$.

steps.slogan: Find a copy of $K_r(t')$ with $t' > t/(r\varepsilon)$ by induction on $r$.
steps.detail: Assume minimum degree at least $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon)n$. Since $1 - 1/r + \varepsilon = 1 - 1/(r-1) + \varepsilon'$ with $\varepsilon' = 1/((r-1)r) + \varepsilon$, the claim for $r - 1$ gives $K_r(t')$ for large $n$. For $r = 1$, $K_1(t')$ is $t'$ isolated vertices.

steps.slogan: Count edges from the copy of $K_r(t')$ to find many vertices with $t$ neighbours in every part.
steps.detail: Each of the $rt'$ vertices of the copy $K$ has at least $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon)n - rt'$ neighbours outside $K$, and an outside vertex with fewer than $t$ neighbours in some part has at most $(r-1)t' + t$ neighbours in $K$. So the set $W$ of outside vertices with $t$ neighbours in every part has $|W|(t' - t) \ge (rt'\varepsilon - t)n - r^2t'^2$, which grows linearly in $n$.

steps.slogan: Give each vertex of $W$ a pattern of $t$-sets and find $t$ vertices with one pattern.
steps.detail: Each $w \in W$ chooses $t$ of its neighbours in each part, one of at most $\binom{t'}{t}^r$ patterns. Once $|W| > (t - 1)\binom{t'}{t}^r$, the pigeonhole principle gives $t$ vertices with the same pattern, and with the $r$ chosen $t$-sets they form a [complete equipartite subgraph](c:complete-equipartite-subgraph) $K_{r+1}(t)$.

steps.slogan: Combine both bounds into $\mathrm{ex}(n, H) = (1 - 1/r + o(1))\, n^2/2$.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives the lower bound. For each $\varepsilon > 0$ and large $n$, a graph with $(1 - 1/r + \varepsilon)\, n^2/2$ edges has by step 3 a large subgraph of high minimum degree, which contains $K_{r+1}(t)$ by steps 4 to 6 and so $H$ by step 1.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem bounds the edges of graphs that avoid $H$.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The chromatic number alone fixes the leading constant $1 - 1/r$.
concepts.c:extremal-number: The extremal number is the quantity that the theorem estimates.
concepts.c:turan-graph: The Turán graph is the extremal example for the lower bound.
concepts.c:complete-equipartite-subgraph: The complete equipartite subgraph is the target that contains $H$.

source.note: Steps 4 to 6 follow mathlib's induction on r with ε' = 1/((r-1)r) + ε, its edge count ErdosStone.filter.pi.exists_le_card_fiber and its pigeonhole step; the deletion step and the Turán lower bound are added for the extremal-number form.

statement: Let $f$ be a [proper convex function](c:proper-convex-function) and $g$ a proper [concave function](c:concave-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose domains have intersecting [relative interiors](c:relative-interior). Then $\inf_x (f(x) - g(x)) = \sup_y (g^*(y) - f^*(y))$, where $f^*$ is the [convex conjugate](c:convex-conjugate) and $g^*(y) = \inf_x (\langle x, y \rangle - g(x))$; the supremum is attained when it is finite.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to (-\infty, \infty]$ is [proper convex](c:proper-convex-function).
The function $g\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to [-\infty, \infty)$ is proper and [concave](c:concave-function).
The [relative interiors](c:relative-interior) of $\mathrm{dom}\, f$ and $\mathrm{dom}\, g$ have a common point.

conclusion: $\inf_x (f(x) - g(x)) = \sup_y (g^*(y) - f^*(y))$, and the supremum is attained when it is finite.

proofs.name: Separation of an epigraph and a hypograph
proofs.slogan: Separate the epigraph of $f$ from the hypograph of $g$ raised by the optimal value, and read the separating hyperplane as a dual solution.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $\alpha = \inf(f - g) = -\infty$, weak duality alone gives equality, and the qualification makes $\alpha < \infty$.

roles.why: Convexity of $f$ makes its epigraph a convex set.
Concavity of $g$ makes its hypograph a convex set.
A common relative interior point makes $\alpha < \infty$ and forbids a vertical separating hyperplane.

steps.slogan: Derive weak duality from the Fenchel-Young inequalities.
steps.detail: The definitions give $f(x) + f^*(y) \ge \langle x, y \rangle \ge g(x) + g^*(y)$, so $f(x) - g(x) \ge g^*(y) - f^*(y)$ for all $x, y$. Hence $\alpha = \inf(f - g) \ge \sup(g^* - f^*)$, with equality when $\alpha = -\infty$.

steps.slogan: Build the epigraph of $f$ and the hypograph of $g + \alpha$ for finite $\alpha$.
steps.detail: A common point of the domains makes $\alpha < \infty$; assume that $\alpha$ is finite. The sets $C_1 = \{(x, t) : t \ge f(x)\}$ and $C_2 = \{(x, t) : t \le g(x) + \alpha\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ are nonempty and [convex](c:convex-set).

steps.slogan: Show that the relative interiors of $C_1$ and $C_2$ are disjoint.
steps.detail: The relative interior of $C_1$ is the set of $(x, t)$ with $x \in \mathrm{ri}\,\mathrm{dom}\, f$ and $t > f(x)$, and that of $C_2$ has $x \in \mathrm{ri}\,\mathrm{dom}\, g$ and $t < g(x) + \alpha$. A common point would give $f(x) < g(x) + \alpha$, against the definition of $\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Separate $C_1$ and $C_2$ properly by a hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
steps.detail: In finite dimension, two nonempty convex sets with disjoint relative interiors have a properly [separating hyperplane](c:separating-hyperplane), one that does not contain both sets. Write it as $\langle x, a \rangle + \lambda t = \beta$, with $C_1$ on the side $\ge \beta$.

steps.slogan: Use the qualification condition to show that the hyperplane is not vertical.
steps.detail: If $\lambda = 0$, then $\langle x, a \rangle \ge \beta$ on $\mathrm{dom}\, f$ and $\le \beta$ on $\mathrm{dom}\, g$, with equality at a common relative interior point; a linear function with an extremum at a relative interior point is constant, so both sets lie in the hyperplane, against proper separation. As $C_1$ is unbounded upward, $\lambda > 0$; scale to $\lambda = 1$.

steps.slogan: Read the hyperplane as an affine function between $f$ and $g + \alpha$.
steps.detail: With $y = -a$, the hyperplane gives $f(x) \ge \langle x, y \rangle + \beta \ge g(x) + \alpha$ for all $x$. So $f^*(y) \le -\beta$ and $g^*(y) \ge \alpha - \beta$, hence $g^*(y) - f^*(y) \ge \alpha$; with step 1, $y$ attains the supremum $\alpha$.

concepts.c:proper-convex-function: Its epigraph is the convex set above the primal objective.
concepts.c:concave-function: Its hypograph is the convex set below the primal objective.
concepts.c:relative-interior: Disjoint relative interiors allow proper separation; a common one blocks vertical hyperplanes.
concepts.c:convex-conjugate: The conjugates measure the best affine minorant and majorant.
concepts.c:convex-set: The epigraph and the raised hypograph are the convex sets to separate.
concepts.c:separating-hyperplane: The separating hyperplane is the graph of the dual affine function.

source.note: R. T. Rockafellar, Convex Analysis, theorem 31.1, proved by proper separation (theorem 11.3).

statement: A smooth [distribution](c:distribution-of-subspaces) $D$ of rank $k$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is involutive, that is, the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) of two vector fields tangent to $D$ is tangent to $D$, if and only if $D$ is [integrable](c:integrable-distribution-of-subspaces): each point has a chart in which $D$ is spanned by $\partial/\partial x^1, \dots, \partial/\partial x^k$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) of dimension $n$.
The field $D$ of $k$-dimensional subspaces $D_p \subseteq T_pM$ is smooth: near each point it is spanned by $k$ smooth vector fields.

conclusion: $D$ is involutive if and only if every point of $M$ has a flat chart for $D$.

proofs.name: Commuting local frame
proofs.slogan: Normalize a local frame of the involutive distribution so that its fields commute, then compose their flows into a flat chart.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the local theorem. The global [foliation](c:foliation) by maximal integral manifolds follows by gluing flat charts and is not covered.

roles.why: Charts of the manifold give coordinate vector fields and a setting for the inverse function theorem.
Smoothness of $D$ gives a smooth local frame, whose flows exist and are smooth.

steps.slogan: Show that a flat chart makes the distribution involutive.
steps.detail: In a flat chart, fields tangent to $D$ are $X = \sum_{i \le k} a^i \partial_i$ and $Y = \sum_{j \le k} b^j \partial_j$. Then $[X, Y] = \sum_{j \le k} (X b^j - Y a^j)\, \partial_j$ is again tangent to $D$, and involutivity is a local property.

steps.slogan: Choose a local frame $X_i = \partial_i + \sum_{j > k} a_i^j \partial_j$ for $D$ near $p$.
steps.detail: Take coordinates at $p$ in which $D_p$ is complementary to the span of $\partial_{k+1}, \dots, \partial_n$. The projection of $D_q$ onto the span of $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_k$ is then an isomorphism for $q$ near $p$, and the preimages of $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_k$ form the frame.

steps.slogan: Use involutivity to show that the frame fields commute.
steps.detail: The coefficients of $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_k$ in each $X_i$ are constants, so the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields) $[X_i, X_l]$ lies in the span of $\partial_{k+1}, \dots, \partial_n$. Involutivity puts it in $D$, which meets that span only in 0, so $[X_i, X_l] = 0$.

steps.slogan: Compose the commuting [flows](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) of the frame into a local parametrization $\Phi$.
steps.detail: Vanishing brackets make the flows $\theta^i$ of the $X_i$ commute. Set $\Phi(t, y) = \theta^1_{t_1} \circ \dots \circ \theta^k_{t_k}(p + (0, y))$ for small $t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k}$; moving $\theta^i$ to the front gives $\partial \Phi / \partial t_i = X_i \circ \Phi$.

steps.slogan: Invert the parametrization by the inverse function theorem to get a flat chart.
steps.detail: At 0 the differential of $\Phi$ sends the coordinate directions to $X_1(p), \dots, X_k(p), \partial_{k+1}, \dots, \partial_n$, a basis, so $\Phi$ is a local diffeomorphism. In the chart $\Phi^{-1}$ the fields $\partial/\partial t_i = X_i$ span $D$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that an [integrable](c:integrable-distribution-of-subspaces) distribution is involutive. Steps 2 to 5 build a flat chart around every point for an involutive distribution, so it is integrable.

concepts.c:distribution-of-subspaces: The distribution is the field of subspaces to be integrated.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The manifold supplies charts and coordinate vector fields.
concepts.c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields: Vanishing brackets of the normalized frame make the flows commute.
concepts.c:integrable-distribution-of-subspaces: Integrability means flat charts exist, which the proof builds.
concepts.c:foliation: Flat charts glue into the foliation of the global version.
concepts.c:flow-of-a-vector-field: Composed flows of the frame give the flat coordinates.

source.note: The commuting-frame proof, as in J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd edition, chapter 19.

statement: Every non-constant [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [complex](c:complex-number) coefficients has a complex [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial).

hypotheses.text: The polynomial $f \in \mathbb{C}[z]$ has [degree](c:degree-of-a-polynomial) $n \ge 1$.

proofs.name: Liouville's theorem
proofs.slogan: If $f$ had no root, $1/f$ would be a bounded entire function that tends to 0 at infinity, so it would vanish identically.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. A nonzero constant has no root, so the hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is necessary.

roles.why: Positive degree makes $|f(z)| \to \infty$ as $|z| \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f$ has no root, so that $1/f$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function).
steps.detail: A polynomial is holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$. If $f(z) \ne 0$ for every $z$, the quotient $1/f$ is holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $|f(z)| \to \infty$ as $|z| \to \infty$.
steps.detail: Write $f(z) = a_n z^n (1 + a_{n-1}/(a_n z) + \dots + a_0/(a_n z^n))$ with $a_n \ne 0$ and $n \ge 1$. The bracket tends to 1, so $|f(z)| \ge |a_n| |z|^n / 2$ for large $|z|$.

steps.slogan: Show by Liouville's theorem that the entire function $1/f$ is identically 0.
steps.detail: By step 2, $1/f(z) \to 0$ as $|z| \to \infty$, so $1/f$ is small outside a large disc and continuous on it; hence $1/f$ is a [bounded function](c:bounded-function). Liouville's theorem makes it constant, and the constant is its limit 0.

steps.slogan: Derive a contradiction from the identity $1/f(z) = 0$.
steps.detail: The reciprocal $1/f(z)$ of a nonzero number is never 0, so step 3 is impossible. Hence the assumption fails, and $f$ has a root.

concepts.c:polynomial: A polynomial is entire and grows like its leading term.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex differentiability is what Liouville's theorem needs.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: A root is the point whose absence leads to a contradiction.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-polynomial: Positive degree forces growth at infinity.
concepts.c:entire-function: Without roots, the reciprocal of $f$ is entire.
concepts.c:bounded-function: Liouville's theorem applies only to bounded entire functions.

proofs.name: Minimum modulus and d'Alembert's lemma
proofs.slogan: The modulus $|f|$ attains a minimum, and at a point where $f \ne 0$ some direction makes $|f|$ smaller.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The step that lowers $|f|$ needs a $k$-th root of a complex number, which the polar form gives.

roles.why: Positive degree gives growth at infinity and a nonzero higher coefficient at the minimum point.

steps.slogan: Find a point $z_0$ where $|f|$ attains its minimum over $\mathbb{C}$.
steps.detail: Since $|f(z)| \to \infty$, there is $R$ with $|f(z)| > |f(0)|$ for $|z| > R$. The continuous function $|f|$ attains a minimum on the compact disc $|z| \le R$, and this minimum is global.

steps.slogan: Expand $f(z_0 + w) = f(z_0) + c w^k + w^{k+1} q(w)$ with $c \ne 0$ and $k \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Expand the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$ in powers of $w = z - z_0$. Since $f$ is not constant, some coefficient after the constant term is nonzero; $c w^k$ is the first such term, and $q$ is a polynomial.

steps.slogan: Choose a direction $\omega$ with $c\omega^k = -f(z_0)$ when $f(z_0) \ne 0$.
steps.detail: The polar form gives a $k$-th root $\omega$ of $-f(z_0)/c$. Then $f(z_0 + s\omega) = f(z_0)(1 - s^k) + O(s^{k+1})$, so $|f(z_0 + s\omega)| < |f(z_0)|$ for small $s > 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the minimum value $f(z_0)$ is 0.
steps.detail: If $f(z_0) \ne 0$, step 3 gives a smaller value of $|f|$, against the minimality from step 1. So $f(z_0) = 0$, and $z_0$ is a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial).

concepts.c:polynomial: The local expansion of a polynomial has finitely many terms.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex $k$-th roots let the proof choose a descent direction.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: The minimum point turns out to be a root.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-polynomial: Positive degree gives growth and a nonconstant expansion.

source.note: Argand's minimum modulus proof through d'Alembert's lemma, a standard textbook route; not the mathlib route.

statement: Let $f$ be $C^1$ near a [hyperbolic equilibrium](c:hyperbolic-equilibrium) $x_0$ of $x' = f(x)$: $f(x_0) = 0$ and no [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of the [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $A = Df(x_0)$ has zero real part. Then a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $h$ from a neighbourhood of $x_0$ onto a neighbourhood of 0 satisfies $h(\varphi_t(x)) = e^{tA} h(x)$ while the orbit stays there, so the flow is locally conjugate to its [linearization](c:linearization).

hypotheses.text: The vector field $f$ is of class $C^1$ on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The point $x_0$ is a [hyperbolic equilibrium](c:hyperbolic-equilibrium): $f(x_0) = 0$ and $Df(x_0)$ has no eigenvalue on the imaginary axis.

conclusion: Near $x_0$ the flow $\varphi_t$ of $f$ is topologically conjugate to the linear flow $e^{tA}$ near 0.

proofs.name: Global perturbation and a functional fixed point
proofs.slogan: Cut off the nonlinearity, conjugate the time-one maps by a fixed point in a space of bounded maps, and average to conjugate the flows.
proofs.scope: An outline; steps 2 to 4 rest on the estimates of the cited work. A translation makes $x_0 = 0$.

roles.why: A $C^1$ field has a derivative at 0 and a nonlinear part with small Lipschitz constant near 0.
Hyperbolicity splits space into contracting and expanding parts of $e^A$, which makes the fixed-point maps contractions.

steps.slogan: Cut off the nonlinear term with a [bump function](c:bump-function) to make it globally small.
steps.detail: Write $f(x) = Ax + g(x)$ with $g(0) = 0$ and $Dg(0) = 0$. Replace $g$ by $\psi(x/\delta)\, g(x)$ for a bump function $\psi$ equal to 1 near 0; for small $\delta$ the new field equals $f$ near 0, and its nonlinear part has a small global Lipschitz constant.

steps.slogan: Compare the time-one maps $L = e^A$ and $T = L + \phi$ of the two flows.
steps.detail: Grönwall's lemma makes $\phi$ bounded with a small Lipschitz constant. No eigenvalue of $A$ has zero real part, so $L$ has no eigenvalue of modulus 1, and $\mathbb{R}^n = E^s \oplus E^u$ with $L$ contracting on $E^s$ and $L^{-1}$ contracting on $E^u$ in an adapted norm.

steps.slogan: Solve $H \circ T = L \circ H$ with $H = I + u$ by a contraction on bounded maps.
steps.detail: The equation reads $u_s = L u_s \circ T^{-1} - \phi_s \circ T^{-1}$ on the stable part and $u_u = L^{-1}(u_u \circ T + \phi_u)$ on the unstable part, a contraction on the Banach space of bounded continuous maps. Its unique fixed point gives $H_0$, a homeomorphism because the same argument builds its inverse.

steps.slogan: Average the map conjugacy along both flows to conjugate the flows.
steps.detail: Set $H = \int_0^1 e^{-sA} H_0\, T^s\, ds$, where $T^s$ is the modified flow. The integrand has period 1 in $s$, so $e^{-tA} H\, T^t = H$ for all $t$; since $H - I$ is bounded, uniqueness in step 3 gives $H = H_0$, so $H_0 \circ T^t = e^{tA} \circ H_0$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the conjugacy to the neighbourhood where the modified field equals $f$.
steps.detail: Near 0 the modified flow agrees with the flow of $f$ while orbits stay there. So $h = H_0$ on a small neighbourhood of 0 is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) onto its image with $h(\varphi_t(x)) = e^{tA} h(x)$, a conjugacy to the [linearization](c:linearization).

concepts.c:hyperbolic-equilibrium: Hyperbolicity is what makes the linear part dominate the flow.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: Eigenvalues off the imaginary axis split space into stable and unstable parts.
concepts.c:jacobian-matrix: The Jacobian at the equilibrium is the linear part $A$.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The conjugacy is only a homeomorphism, not a diffeomorphism in general.
concepts.c:linearization: The theorem compares the flow with its linearization $e^{tA}$.
concepts.c:bump-function: The bump function makes the nonlinearity globally small.

source.ref: P. Hartman, A lemma in the theory of structural stability of differential equations, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 11 (1960), 610-620

statement: Let $F_1, \dots, F_m$ be [convex sets](c:convex-set) in a real vector space of [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) $d$, with $m \ge d + 1$. If every $d + 1$ of them have a common point, then all $m$ of them have a common point.

hypotheses.text: Each set $F_i$ is a [convex](c:convex-set) subset of a real vector space of [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) $d$.
The family has $m \ge d + 1$ sets.
Every $d + 1$ of the sets have a common point.

formal.difference: The declaration works in any finite-dimensional vector space over a linearly ordered field, with $d$ its dimension; otherwise it states the same.

proofs.name: Induction with Radon points
proofs.slogan: Induct on the number of sets, take for each set a point in all the others, and show that a Radon point of these points lies in every set.
proofs.scope: Every $m \ge d + 1$; the case $m = d + 1$ is the hypothesis. The sets need not be closed or bounded, because the family is finite.

roles.why: Convexity puts the convex hull of points of $F_k$ inside $F_k$.
With $m \ge d + 1$, every smaller subfamily extends to one of exactly $d + 1$ sets.
Each subfamily of $d + 1$ sets has a common point.

steps.slogan: Show that every subfamily of at most $d + 1$ sets has a common point.
steps.detail: Since $m \ge d + 1$, a subfamily with at most $d + 1$ sets lies inside a subfamily of exactly $d + 1$ sets. A common point of the larger subfamily is a common point of the smaller one.

steps.slogan: For $m \ge d + 2$, pick for each $i$ a point $x_i$ common to all $F_j$ with $j \ne i$.
steps.detail: Induct on $m$, for families in which every subfamily of at most $d + 1$ sets meets; the base $m = d + 1$ is step 1. For $m \ge d + 2$, the $m - 1$ sets $F_j$ with $j \ne i$ form such a family, so by induction they have a common point $x_i$.

steps.slogan: Split the $m \ge d + 2$ points by Radon's theorem into two parts with a common hull point.
steps.detail: More than $d + 1$ points in dimension $d$ are not [affinely independent](c:affine-independence), so Radon's theorem gives a partition $I \sqcup J$ of the indices and a point $z$ in the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $\{x_i : i \in I\}$ and in that of $\{x_j : j \in J\}$.

concepts.c:convex-set: Convex sets contain the hulls of their points, which traps the Radon point.
concepts.c:dimension-of-a-vector-space: The dimension $d$ fixes the number $d + 1$ in the hypothesis.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The Radon point lies in two convex hulls at once.
concepts.c:affine-independence: Too many points are affinely dependent, which Radon's theorem needs.

statement: If $H$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$, then the [order](c:order-of-a-group) of $H$ divides the order of $G$. More precisely $|G| = [G : H]\, |H|$, where the [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $[G : H]$ is the number of left [cosets](c:coset) of $H$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is [finite](c:finite-group).
The set $H$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the divisibility and uses Nat.card, which is 0 for an infinite type, so it also holds, trivially, for infinite groups.

proofs.name: Coset partition
proofs.slogan: The left cosets of $H$ partition $G$ into blocks that all have $|H|$ elements.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the trivial subgroup and $H = G$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the orders and the number of cosets natural numbers.
The subgroup axioms make the coset relation an equivalence relation.

steps.slogan: Define $x \sim y$ by $x^{-1}y \in H$ and check that it is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation).
steps.detail: The identity of $H$ gives $x \sim x$, inverses in $H$ give symmetry because $(x^{-1}y)^{-1} = y^{-1}x$, and closure under products gives transitivity. The class of $x$ is the left [coset](c:coset) $xH$.

steps.slogan: Show that each left coset $xH$ has exactly $|H|$ elements.
steps.detail: The map $h \mapsto xh$ from $H$ to $xH$ is surjective by the definition of $xH$. It is injective by left cancellation, because $xh = xh'$ implies $h = h'$, so it is a bijection.

steps.slogan: Count $G$ as a disjoint union of $[G : H]$ cosets of size $|H|$.
steps.detail: The equivalence classes partition the finite set $G$ into $[G : H]$ cosets, and each has $|H|$ elements by step 2. So $|G| = [G : H]\, |H|$, and $|H|$ divides $|G|$.

concepts.c:subgroup: The subgroup axioms make the cosets a partition.
concepts.c:finite-group: In a finite group the counting gives natural numbers.
concepts.c:order-of-a-group: The theorem compares the orders of $H$ and $G$.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: The index is the number of blocks in the partition.
concepts.c:coset: Cosets are the equal-sized blocks that partition $G$.
concepts.c:equivalence-relation: Its classes are the cosets, so they are disjoint.

statement: Let $H(q, p)$ be a $C^2$ [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) on the [phase space](c:phase-space) $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, and let a $C^1$ density $\rho(q, p, t)$ satisfy the [continuity equation](c:continuity-equation) $\partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = 0$ for the [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) $v = (\partial H/\partial p, -\partial H/\partial q)$. Then $\partial_t \rho + \{\rho, H\} = 0$, so $\rho$ is constant along every trajectory.

hypotheses.text: The [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) $H$ is of class $C^2$ on the phase space.
The density $\rho$ is of class $C^1$ and satisfies the [continuity equation](c:continuity-equation) for the velocity field $v = (\partial H/\partial p, -\partial H/\partial q)$.

conclusion: $\partial_t \rho + \{\rho, H\} = 0$, and $\rho(q(t), p(t), t)$ is constant along each solution of Hamilton's equations.

proofs.name: Divergence-free Hamiltonian field
proofs.slogan: The Hamiltonian vector field has zero divergence, so the continuity equation reduces to transport along the flow.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; the same computation works for a time-dependent Hamiltonian.

roles.why: Two continuous derivatives make the mixed partial derivatives of $H$ equal.
The continuity equation is the identity that the proof rewrites.

steps.slogan: Show that the [Hamiltonian vector field](c:hamiltonian-vector-field) has zero [divergence](c:divergence).
steps.detail: The divergence is $\nabla \cdot v = \sum_i (\partial^2 H/\partial q_i \partial p_i - \partial^2 H/\partial p_i \partial q_i)$. It is 0 because the mixed partial derivatives of a $C^2$ function are equal.

steps.slogan: Expand the divergence term of the continuity equation by the product rule.

The product rule gives $

steps.slogan: Identify $v \cdot \nabla \rho$ with the [Poisson bracket](c:poisson-bracket) $\{\rho, H\}$.
steps.detail: Written out, $v \cdot \nabla \rho = \sum_i (\partial \rho/\partial q_i\, \partial H/\partial p_i - \partial \rho/\partial p_i\, \partial H/\partial q_i) = \{\rho, H\}$. So $\partial_t \rho + \{\rho, H\} = 0$, which is Liouville's equation.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $\rho$ along a trajectory to see that it stays constant.
steps.detail: Along a solution of $\dot q = \partial H/\partial p$, $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt} \rho(q(t), p(t), t) = \partial_t \rho + \dot q \cdot \nabla_q \rho + \dot p \cdot \nabla_p \rho = \partial_t \rho + \{\rho, H\} = 0$.

concepts.c:hamiltonian: The Hamiltonian generates the velocity field of the flow.
concepts.c:phase-space: The density lives on phase space, the space of positions and momenta.
concepts.c:continuity-equation: Conservation of probability is the starting identity.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-vector-field: Its divergence vanishes, which removes the compression term.
concepts.c:divergence: Zero divergence turns the continuity equation into a transport equation.
concepts.c:poisson-bracket: The transport term is exactly the Poisson bracket with $H$.
